newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BOC puts health business up for sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BOC puts health business up for sale.

text.p: British gases company BOC Group Plc hung a for sale sign on its Ohmeda healthcare business on Wednesday, delighting investors who pushed its shares up to record levels.
The decision marked the end of years of effort by BOC to turn its medical gases and critical monitoring equipment arm around.

BOC chief executive Danny Rosenkranz told Reuters Ohmeda had reached a crossroads. "BOC now has a choice - either to sell it... or put serious money into it," said Rosenkranz, adding he would rather pump cash into BOC's industrial gases business.

Analysts said the sale was likely bring in anything between 500 million pounds ($839.4 million) and one billion pounds, helping BOC build on its position as one of the world's biggest and most successful producers of industrial gases like oxygen, nitrogen and argon.
Shares soared to record highs, gaining seven percent or 75 pence to 1147 1/2 pence in midmorning trading.

"This is the first stage of the rerating," said Nikko Europe analyst Philip Morrish. "This is what shareholders wanted. The rating will be much higher the closer they get to being a pure gases company."
The writing has been on the wall for some time for Ohmeda, which saw its sales drop nine percent in the six months to March to 226.3 million pounds and profits slip eight percent to 26.1 million.

Its major markets have been going through a tough time, particularly in the U.S. where pressure on healthcare budgets has been fierce. The business was delivered a serious blow earlier this year when U.S. regulators extended a patent on Zeneca Group Plc anaesthetic Diprivan, torpedoing well-advanced plans to launch a generic rival.

"It has been a weight around the group's neck for a long time," said Nikko's Morrish. "They have thrown money at it and it's not worked, and they've rationalised and rationalised and it's not worked."

Analysts said BOC lacked critical mass to make a success of the business, which accounted for less than 12 percent of first-half sales. However general restructuring in the world's healthcare sector means BOC should have no shortage of buyers.

"This could be one of those deals when BOC may be able to sell for a pretty high price and it would still be a good price for the right purchaser," said SocGen analyst Paul Diggle, who added that a billion pounds, or roughly twice annual sales, could be possible.
The buyer will acquire major positions in anaesthetic gases, a market dominated for years by BOC's Forane which has been ravaged by generic competition since 1993.

The follow-up gas, Suprane, is steadily gaining market share, and a promising new product for treating respiratory problems in new-born infants, known as blue-baby syndrome, is currently being considered by U.S. regulators.
Analysts said cash from the sale would allow BOC to chase growth opportunities in its industrial gas operations, which require heavy up-front investment.

Although Rosenkranz told Reuters he had no major acquisitions in mind, there has been speculation that BOC could be interested in the Swedish gases business AGA AB, which has around eight percent of the world market compared to around 16 percent for BOC. The two businesses are seen as a good geographical fit.
